teaser.en: At Kibuyuni, women who were traditionally kept from fishing now farm the sea, and turn their seaweed into soap, lotion and juice.

summary.en: Spinosum is a spiny red-brown seaweed farmed in the shallow lagoons of the south coast, mostly by women. Dried and sold for carrageenan, or made into soaps and lotions, it has become an important source of income at Kibuyuni near Shimoni.

about.en: Spinosum is a red alga, not a true plant, with branching stems that are red-brown and covered in short spines. It grows quickly from small cuttings, and a farmer can harvest it about every six weeks. It is rich in carrageenan, a natural gel used to thicken foods and cosmetics.

where.en: It is farmed on off-bottom lines and stakes in the shallow lagoons at Kibuyuni near Shimoni and in other south-coast villages. The Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute (KMFRI) has run a model farm there since 2012. At low tide, the rows of stakes and ropes are easy to see from the shore.

uses.en:
Farmers tie cuttings to ropes stretched between stakes in the shallows, then harvest the seaweed about six weeks later, dry it and sell it as a source of carrageenan.

The women of Kibuyuni also add value to their harvest themselves, making soap, body lotion, shampoo, juice and hair food from it.

culture.en: Seaweed farming on the south coast is mostly women's work: about three in four farmers are women, who traditionally could not fish. It has given them their own income from the sea. The Kibuyuni farmers' group became a cooperative in 2019.

names.en: No Digo name has been recorded yet. In Swahili, farmed seaweed is *mwani*. In English it is spinosum seaweed, and its scientific name is *Eucheuma denticulatum*.

conservation.en: It is a farmed crop. Harvests suffer in warm-water die-offs and from 'ice-ice' disease, which bleaches and kills the seaweed.

reason.en: The other carrageenan seaweed farmed alongside it
Grows in the same shallow lagoons
Another key source of income on the coast
